items.title: Jimmy and Jeannie Cheatham interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 12, 1998
items.q: we told her what ideas we had about bringing Big Mama and Sippie Wallace and myself together — three generations of the blues... Big Mama would do hers. And then I would do mine. And at the end of mine we’d do a finale.

ctx.x: Tell me about the PBS Special you did with Sippie Wallace.

And Big Mama? That was our concept. And this lady at KPBS came to us and asked if we wanted to do some kind of special or what we wanted to do. She said it would be a half hour. And so we told her what ideas we had about bringing Big Mama and Sippie Wallace and myself together — three generations of the blues. So she worked very hard, and we got this thing going. And it was the rainiest day. We were doing a jam session, still, and we set it up so that Sippie would do the first, a whole show, an hour. This was at…
Tavern. Which is up north in Solana Beach.

items.title: Jimmy and Jeannie Cheatham interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 12, 1998
items.q: And I played with Big Mama Thornton

ctx.x: No. Jimmy Rushing. But none of them had music. They never had any music. And I was used to reading everything see? So I said, “Well I don’t know that song.” He said, “It goes like this,” and he sits down to play more piano than most piano players. A very excellent pianist. Show me the bridge [scats] — whooo, okay. But he was very nice. And I played with Big Mama Thornton and they were all—

items.title: Jimmy and Jeannie Cheatham interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 12, 1998
items.q: I had played for Big Mama all these years and she had never heard me sing.

ctx.x: How that was going to go down.

Because they are very ornery people, both of them, and we didn’t want them to throw anything into the works. So Sippie, she did hers, and Big Mama did hers, and then when I did mine, then I said, “Ladies and Gentlemen, now we’re going to have a good old fashioned finale. And we’re going to call up these ladies, Sippie Wallace and Big Mama Thorton.” They stopped. They were at the bottom of the step watching me because they had never heard me sing. And I had played for Big Mama all these years and she had never…
She didn’t even know she could sing.
